farraa:3-3.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿غَافِرِ ٱلذَّنبِ وَقَابِلِ ٱلتَّوْبِ شَدِيدِ ٱلْعِقَابِ﴾.
He made them like an adjective (naʿt) of a definite noun, though they are indefinite; do you not see that you say: marartu bi-rajulin shadīdi al-qalbi ("I passed by a man strong of heart")? Except that together with them came His words ﴿ذى الطول﴾, which is definite, so they were made to run in its course. Their genitive may also be by repetition (takrīr, i.e. as a badal (substitute)), in which case definite and indefinite are the same. Similar are His words: ﴿وَهُوَ الْغَفُورُ الوَدُودُ، ذُو العرشِ المجيدُ، فعَّالٌ لما يريدُ﴾: this is by repetition, [163/ا] because faʿʿāl is purely indefinite. Similar are His words: ﴿رفيعُ الدرجاتِ ذو العرشِ﴾: rafīʿ is indefinite, and it was made to run as a fresh start (istiʾnāf), or on the explanation of the first case.

farraa:5-5.t:
His words: ﴿وَهَمَّتْ كُـلُّ أُمَّةٍ بِرَسُولِهِمْ﴾.
He referred it to the men. In the reading (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh it is "bi-rasūlihā" ("its messenger"), and all is correct.

farraa:8-8.t:
His words: ﴿وَأَدْخِلْهُمْ جَنَّاتِ عَدْنٍ﴾.
Some read "jannata ʿadnin" in the singular, and so it is in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: singular.
His words: ﴿وَمَن صَـلَحَ مِنْ آبَآئِهِمْ﴾.
man is accusative from two possible places: if you wish you may make (wa-man) refer back to the hāʾ and mīm in "wa-adkhilhum", and if you wish to the hāʾ and mīm in "waʿadtahum".

farraa:10-10.t:
His words: ﴿يُنَادَوْنَ لَمَقْتُ ٱللَّهِ﴾.
The meaning in it is: they will be called out to that Allah's loathing of you is greater than your loathing of yourselves on the Day of Resurrection; for they loathed themselves since they had abandoned faith. But the lām suffices instead of saying, in speech: nādaytu anna Zaydan qāʾimun ("I proclaimed that Zayd is standing"), and nādaytu la-Zaydun qāʾimun. Similar is: ﴿ثم بَدا لهم من بعدِ ما رَأوا الآياتِ﴾ (the verse). The lām is equivalent to anna in every expression resembling "saying", such as "they are called out to", "they are told", and the like.

farraa:15-15.t:
His words: ﴿يُلْقِي ٱلرُّوحَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ عَلَىٰ مَن يَشَآءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ﴾.
"The Spirit" in this place is prophethood: so that the one upon whom He casts the Spirit may warn of the Day of Meeting. It is called "the Meeting" (al-talāq) only because the people of heaven and the people of earth meet in it.

farraa:16-16.t:
His words: ﴿يَوْمَ هُم بَارِزُونَ﴾.
hum is in the position of a nominative by its predicate after it, and [it is] like your saying: ātīka yawma anta fārighun lī ("I will come to you on the day you are free for me").

farraa:18-18.t:
His words: ﴿ٱلأَزِفَةِ﴾.
It is the Resurrection.
His words: ﴿كَاظِمِينَ﴾.
It is accusative by qaṭʿ (detachment) from the meaning that refers back to them in "the hearts" and "the throats"; the meaning is: when their hearts are at their throats, suppressing [their grief]. If you wish you may make its detachment from the hāʾ in His words "wa-andhirhum"; the first is better in Arabic.
Had it been "kāẓimūna", nominative, on your saying: "when the hearts are at the throats, when they are suppressing", or as a fresh start, it would have been correct.
His words: ﴿مَا لِلظَّالِمِينَ مِنْ حَمِيمٍ وَلاَ شَفِيعٍ يُطَاعُ﴾:
whose intercession is accepted. Then He said: ﴿يَعْلَمُ خَآئِنَةَ ٱلأَعْيُنِ﴾, meaning Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is said: a man has two glances: the first is permitted to him and the second is forbidden to him. So His words ﴿يعلم خائنة﴾ al-aʿyun refer to the second glance, and "what the breasts conceal" to the first glance. If the first glance was deliberate, there is sin in it too; and if he did not intend it, it is forgiven.

farraa:26-26.t:
His words: ﴿أَوْ أَن يُظْهِرَ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ ٱلْفَسَادَ﴾.
Al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim made (الفَسَاد) nominative, making the verb belong to it [yaẓhara al-fasādu, "that corruption appear"]. The people of Medina and al-Sulamī read: [wa-an] yuẓhira fī al-arḍi al-fasāda, making "corruption" accusative and making yuẓhira [the act] of Moses. The people of Medina drop the first alif, saying: wa-an yuẓhira, and so [it is] in their codices; while in the codices of the people of Iraq: "aw an yaẓhara". [The meaning] is that he said: I fear a change [163/ب] to your religion, or that people will hear [of it] and believe him, so that there will be corruption to your religion in it.

farraa:32-32.t:
His words: ﴿[وَ] يٰقَوْمِ إِنِّيۤ أَخَافُ عَلَيْكُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلتَّنَادِ﴾.
The common people read it al-tanādi, light [without doubling]; al-Ḥasan alone kept the yāʾ [in it]. It is from tanādā al-qawm ("the people called out to one another"). [Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us:] al-Farrāʾ related to us; he said: Ḥibbān related to me from al-Ajlaḥ, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim, that he said: The angels will descend from the heavens and surround the regions of the earth, and Hell will be brought; when they see it, it will terrify them, and they will flee (nadda) in the earth as camels flee, but they will not head for any region without seeing angels, so they will return to where they came from. That is His words: ﴿يَا مَعْشَرَ الْجِنِّ والإِنْسِ إِنِ اسْتَطَعْتُمْ أَنْ تنفذوا من أقطار السماواتِ والأرضِ﴾, and that is His words: ﴿وجَاءَ رَبُّكَ وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا، وَجِىءَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِجَهَنَّمَ﴾, and that is His words: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السَّمَاءُ بِالْغَمَامِ وَنُزِّلَ الْمَلاَئِكَةُ تَنْزِيلاً﴾. Al-Ajlaḥ said: and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read it "al-tanādd" with the dāl doubled. Ḥibbān said: and so al-Kalbī explained it, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās.
Al-Farrāʾ said: And whoever reads it "التَّنَاد" [light] means the day when the people of Paradise call out to the people of the Fire, and the people of the Fire to the people of Paradise, and the people of the Heights to men whom they recognize.

farraa:35-35.t:
His words: ﴿كَبُرَ مَقْتاً عِندَ ٱللَّهِ﴾.
That is: that disputing is grievous as an object of loathing [tamyīz (specification)]. Similar is: ﴿كَبُرَتْ كَلِمَةً تَخْرُجُ مِنْ أَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾: in kaburat their saying ﴿اتَّخَذَ اللّهُ وَلَداً﴾ is implied. Whoever makes "word" nominative implies nothing; al-Ḥasan read it so, with "word" nominative: ﴿كَبُرَتْ كَلِمَةٌ تَخْرُجُ﴾.
His words: ﴿عَلَىٰ كُـلِّ قَلْبِ مُتَكَبِّرٍ جَبَّارٍ﴾: He puts "heart" in iḍāfa to "the arrogant one". Whoever uses tanwīn makes the heart itself the arrogant tyrant. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "kadhālika yaṭbaʿu Allāhu ʿalā qalbi kulli mutakabbirin jabbārin" ("on the heart of every arrogant tyrant"); this is a witness for whoever reads with iḍāfa. The meaning, whether "heart" comes first or later, is the same, and Allah knows best.
He said: I heard one of the Arabs [say]: "He combs his hair on the day of every Friday", meaning "every Friday day"; and the meaning is the same.

farraa:36-37.t:
His words: ﴿لَّعَـلِّيۤ أَبْلُغُ ٱلأَسْبَابَ (أَسْبَابَ ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ) فَأَطَّلِعُ﴾.
With the nominative [fa-aṭṭaliʿu], referring it back to His words "ablughu". Whoever makes it an answer to laʿallī makes it accusative [fa-aṭṭaliʿa], and some readers read it so. He said: and one of the Arabs recited to me:
علَّ صروفَ الدَّهر أو دولاتها * يدللنا اللَّمَّةَ من لَمَّاتها * فتستريحَ النفسُ من زَفْراتها *
(Perhaps the turns of fortune or its changes will bring us round to one of its visitations, so that the soul may rest from its sighs.)
He used the accusative as the answer to laʿalla.

farraa:46-46.t:
His words: ﴿ٱلنَّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْهَا﴾.
You make (al-nār) nominative by what refers back to it in ʿalayhā. Had you made it nominative by what makes ﴿سُوءَ الْعَذَاب﴾ (45) nominative [i.e. as a badal (substitute) of it], it would have been correct. And had you made it accusative, on the ground that it falls [164/ا] between something referring back to it and speech connected with what precedes it, it would have been correct. Similar is: ﴿قُلْ أَفَأُنَبِّئكُمْ بِشَرٍّ مِنْ ذَلِكُم النارُ وَعَدهَا﴾.
His words: ﴿غُدُوًّا وَعَشِيًّا﴾.
In the Hereafter there is neither morning nor evening; rather, it is the measures of the evenings and mornings of this world.
His words: ﴿[وَ] يَوْمَ تَقُومُ ٱلسَّاعَةُ أَدْخِلُوۤاْ آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾.
Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and the people of the Ḥijāz pronounced the alif with hamza [adkhilū], while ʿĀṣim and al-Ḥasan made it light, reading "wa-yawma taqūmu al-sāʿatu udkhulū āla Firʿawna"; here "the family of Pharaoh" is accusative as a vocative: "Enter, O family of Pharaoh, the severest punishment". In the first case "adkhilū" falls upon them [as its object].

farraa:48-48.t:
His words: ﴿إِنَّا كُلٌّ فِيهَآ﴾.
You make (kull) nominative by fīhā, and do not make it an adjective of innā. And if you made it accusative on that basis [as tawkīd (emphasis)], making [fīhā] the predicate of innā «[Translator's note: the apodosis is missing in the source; presumably "it would be correct"]». Similar is: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّ الأَمْرَ كُلَّهُ لِلّهِ﴾: you make ﴿كلّه لله﴾ nominative, and you make it accusative on this explanation.

farraa:51-51.t:
His words: ﴿وَيَوْمَ يَقُومُ ٱلأَشْهَادُ﴾.
The readers read with yāʾ, meaning yaqūmu in the masculine. Had a reader read "wa-yawma taqūmu", it would have been correct [Translator's note: the source prints «صوبا», a misprint for «صوابا»], because al-ashhād is a plural, and a plural of a masculine may have its verb feminine or masculine when the verb comes first. The Arabs say: dhahabat al-rijāl and dhahaba al-rijāl ("the men went").

farraa:56-56.t:
His words: ﴿إِلاَّ كِبْرٌ مَّـا هُم بِبَالِغِيهِ﴾.
He means: they were too proud to believe in what Muḥammad, Allah bless him, brought; they will not attain that, i.e. they will not obtain what they wanted.

farraa:67-67.t:
His words: ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَكُـونُواْ شُيُوخاً﴾.
In the reading (ḥarf) of ʿAbd Allāh: "wa-minkum man yakūnu shuyūkhan" ("and among you are those who become old men"): He made the verb of man singular, then returned to "old men", intending the plural by man. Had He said "shaykhan" (singular), because man is singular in wording, it would have been correct.

farraa:71-71.t:
His words: ﴿إِذِ ٱلأَغْلاَلُ فِيۤ أَعْنَاقِهِمْ وٱلسَّلاَسِلُ﴾.
[You make "the chains" and "the shackles" nominative. And had you made "the chains" accusative and said: "yusḥabūna" (active: yasḥabūna), you would mean] they drag their chains in Hell.
Al-Kalbī mentioned from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: "[and they] are dragged in the chains". The genitive of "the chains" is not permissible, since the preposition would be implied; but had someone imagining it said: "the meaning is only: when their necks are in the shackles, and in the chains they are dragged", the genitive in "the chains" would be permissible on this approach. Similar, among what was referred back to the meaning, is the poet's saying:
قد سالم الحياتِ منه القدَما * الأُفعوانَ والشُّجاعَ الشجعما
(His foot has made peace with the snakes — the viper and the bold, fierce serpent.)
He made "the serpent" (al-shujāʿ) accusative, while "the snakes" before it are nominative «[Translator's note: the verse as printed in the source vowels الحياتِ with kasra, i.e. accusative]», because the meaning is: his foot made peace with the snakes and they made peace with it; when he needed the rhyme to be accusative, he made the verb of the foot fall upon the snakes.
